claim: Granule cell precursors (GCPs) robustly express p75NTR in the external granule layer (EGL) when they are proliferating during postnatal development.
source: Our results show that granule cell precursors (GCPs) robustly express p75NTR in the external granule layer (EGL) when they are proliferating during postnatal development
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing p75NTR expression in proliferating GCPs in the EGL (Figure 1C-F) and Western blot analysis (Figure 2).

claim: GCPs do not express p75NTR when they migrate from the rhombic lip during embryonic development.
source: however, they do not express p75NTR when they migrate either from the rhombic lip during embryonic development
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry showing absence of p75NTR in migrating cells from the rhombic lip at E13.5 (Figure 1A-B).

claim: GCPs do not express p75NTR when they migrate from the EGL during postnatal development.
source: or from the EGL during postnatal development
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry showing no overlap between p75NTR and migratory markers DCX and TAG1 (Figure 1D-F).

claim: p75NTR prevents GCP migration by maintaining elevated levels of active RhoA.
source: We show that p75NTR prevented GCP migration by maintaining elevated levels of active RhoA.
evidence: Supported by data showing p75NTR-/- cells have reduced active RhoA (Figure 7A), overexpression of constitutively active RhoA blocks migration (Figure 7D), and RhoA inhibition rescues migration in p75NTR-overexpressing cells (Figure 7F).

claim: The expression of p75NTR is sufficient to prevent the migration of granule cells even in the presence of BDNF.
source: The expression of p75NTR was sufficient to prevent the migration of the granule cells even in the presence of BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor), a well-established chemotactic signal for this cell population.
evidence: Supported by transwell assay data showing p75NTR overexpression blocks BDNF-induced migration (Figure 5E-F) and time-lapse microscopy in organotypic slices (Figure 5G).

claim: At E13.5, granule cell precursors expressing PAX6 do not express the neuronal migratory marker DCX.
source: During early embryonic development (E13.5) the precursors of the granule cells, indicated by the expression of PAX6 (Figure 1A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, magenta), begin to disperse rostrally from the rhombic lip. Interestingly, these precursor cells do not express the neuronal migratory marker DCX (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, white)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At E13.5, no expression of p75NTR was observed in the migrating cells from the rhombic lip.
source: During this period, no expression of p75NTR was observed in the migrating cells (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, green).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At E15.5, a subpopulation of cells in the internal part of the migratory stream expresses both PAX6 and p75NTR.
source: At later stages (E15.5) the majority of the precursor cells still migrate tangentially to complete the formation of the EGL. However, a subpopulation of cells begins to emerge, located in the internal part of the migratory stream, these cells express PAX6 (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, magenta) and the neurotrophin receptor p75NTR (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, green).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At E17.5, there is an enlargement of the EGL accompanied by an increase in the number of p75NTR expressing cells.
source: At the final stages of embryonic development (E17.5), there is an enlargement of the EGL, which is accompanied by an increase in the number of p75NTR expressing cells (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, green)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of p75NTR closely correlates with the proliferation levels in the EGL, with a peak during maximal proliferation at P5-7 in mice.
source: Moreover, the expression of p75NTR closely correlates with the proliferation levels in the EGL, with a peak of p75NTR expression during the maximal proliferation stage of the GCPs, which in mice occurs around P5–7 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing colocalization of p75NTR with Ki67 in Figure 1C.

claim: Postmitotic GCPs downregulate the expression of p75NTR.
source: In contrast to the expression of p75NTR in proliferating cells, postmitotic cells downregulate the expression of p75NTR
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry showing no overlap between p75NTR and migratory markers TAG1 or DCX (Figure 1D-F).

claim: No overlap between p75NTR and the migratory markers TAG1 or DCX was observed.
source: and no overlap between p75NTR and the migratory markers was observed (Figure 1D–F)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: Shh is a well-known mitogen for GCPs.
source: In the presence of Shh, a well-known mitogen for GCPs (Wallace, 1999; Kenney and Rowitch, 2000)
evidence: Supported by citations to Wallace, 1999 and Kenney and Rowitch, 2000.

claim: In the presence of Shh, GCPs are maintained in a proliferative and undifferentiated state with high expression levels of PCNA.
source: In the presence of Shh, a well-known mitogen for GCPs (Wallace, 1999; Kenney and Rowitch, 2000), these cells are maintained in a proliferative and undifferentiated state with high expression levels of the proliferation marker PCNA (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: As early as 24 hr in culture without Shh, there is a significant reduction in the level of PCNA.
source: However, as early as 24 hr in culture without Shh, there is a significant reduction in the level of PCNA.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: p75NTR expression significantly decreased in conditions without Shh.
source: We also observed that p75NTR expression significantly decreased in conditions without Shh
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: p75NTR expression remained elevated in the proliferative environment induced by Shh.
source: but remained elevated in the proliferative environment induced by Shh (Figure 2A and C)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: Shh induced a dose-dependent increase in proliferation, estimated by the number of Ki67+ cells.
source: Shh induced a dose-dependent increase in proliferation, estimated by the number of Ki67+ cells (Figure 2G top panels, 2H)
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry and quantification data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: Shh induced a dose-dependent increase in PCNA expression.
source: and the relative increase in PCNA expression (Figure 2D and E)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Shh maintained high expression levels of p75NTR in a dose-dependent manner.
source: At the same time, Shh maintained high expression levels of p75NTR in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2G middle panels, 2D, F, J).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 2D, F, G, J.

claim: The number of double-labeled cells expressing p75 and Ki67 increased in response to Shh in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Consistent with the observations in the EGL during cerebellar development (Figure 1), the number of double-labeled cells expressing p75 and Ki67 also increased in response to Shh in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry and quantification data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: All the proliferating cells expressed p75NTR, even in control conditions.
source: Furthermore, all the proliferating cells also expressed p75NTR, even in the control conditions where the few remaining proliferating cells also expressed p75NTR (Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry and quantification data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: ProNT-3 can induce cell cycle exit of GCPs via p75NTR, even in the presence of Shh.
source: Previously, we have shown that proNT-3 can induce cell cycle exit of GCPs via p75NTR, even in the presence of Shh (Zanin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zanin et al., 2016.

claim: ProNT-3 induced a reduction in Ki67+ cells.
source: Confirming the cell cycle withdrawal induced by proNT-3, we observed a reduction in the Ki67+ cells
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: ProNT-3 induced a significant decrease in p75NTR expression.
source: which was accompanied by a significant decrease in p75NTR expression (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: ProNT-3 induced an increase in the levels of βIII-tubulin even in the presence of SAG.
source: Consistent with increased differentiation, proNT-3 induced an increase in the levels of βIII-tubulin even in the presence of SAG (Figure 3A and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3A and D.

claim: PACAP is a known anti-mitogenic ligand for GCPs.
source: we treated granule cells with PACAP, a known anti-mitogenic ligand for GCPs (Nicot et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Nicot et al., 2002.

claim: PACAP induced a dose-dependent reduction in Ki67 levels.
source: PACAP induced a dose-dependent reduction in Ki67 (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: PACAP induced a dose-dependent reduction in PCNA levels.
source: and PCNA levels (Figure 3I–J)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3I-J.

claim: PACAP induced a concomitant reduction in p75NTR expression in a dose-dependent manner, even in the presence of SAG.
source: and a concomitant reduction in p75NTR expression in a dose-dependent manner, even in the presence of SAG (Figure 3E, G, I, K)
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 3E, G, I, K.

claim: The reduced proliferation induced by PACAP was accompanied by increased neuronal differentiation, indicated by an increase in the levels of βIII-tubulin.
source: The reduced proliferation induced by PACAP was accompanied by increased neuronal differentiation, indicated by an increase in the levels of βIII-tubulin (Figures 3E, H, 2).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3E and H.

claim: Cells that were maintained continuously in the presence of SAG for 48 hr continued to proliferate, regardless of the transfected construct (Ctrl-GFP or p75-GFP).
source: As expected, cells that were maintained continuously in the presence of SAG for 48 hr continued to proliferate, regardless of the transfected construct (i.e. Ctrl-GFP or p75-GFP; Figure 4A right panels, 4B-F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 4A-F.

claim: Both transfected and non-transfected cells cultured in the absence of the mitogen for 48 hr did not proliferate.
source: Similarly, both transfected and non-transfected cells cultured in the absence of the mitogen for 48 hr did not proliferate (Figure 4A left panels, 4B–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 4A-F.

claim: When cells were cultured without SAG for the first 24 hr and then with SAG for the next 24 hr, there was no significant difference in the proliferation response between the Ctrl-GFP or p75-GFP transfected cells.
source: Interestingly, when cells were cultured without SAG for the first 24 hr, and then with SAG for the next 24 hr, there was no significant difference in the proliferation response between the Ctrl-GFP or p75-GFP transfected cells.
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 4A-F.

claim: There was no difference in proliferation between cells maintained without SAG for the first 24 hr then with SAG for 24 hr and cells maintained in the absence of SAG for the entire 48 hr.
source: Moreover, there was no difference between this condition and the cells maintained in the absence of SAG for the entire 48 hr (Figure 4A middle panels, 4B–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 4A-F.

claim: There was a significant reduction in proliferation levels in the cells maintained without the mitogen during the first 24 hr in culture, and the re-exposure to SAG did not induce re-entry to the cell cycle.
source: Consistently, there was a significant reduction in proliferation levels in the cells maintained without the mitogen during the first 24 hr in culture, and the re-exposure to SAG did not induce re-entry to the cell cycle (Figure 4B, C and F)
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 4B, C, and F.

claim: The continued expression of p75NTR is not sufficient to maintain the CGPs in a proliferative state.
source: indicating that the continued expression of p75NTR is not sufficient to maintain the CGPs in a proliferative state, thus unresponsive to the delayed SAG addition.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing that p75NTR overexpression did not allow cells to re-enter the cell cycle upon SAG re-addition (Figure 4).

claim: p75NTR-/- cells showed a twofold increase in the number of migrating cells compared to WT cells in a transwell migration assay.
source: The p75NTR-/- cells showed a twofold increase in the number of migrating cells compared to WT cells (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: BDNF is a well-known chemoattractant for postmitotic CGNs.
source: and stimulated migration using brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) (Figure 5C right panels, Figure 5D), a well-known chemoattractant for the postmitotic CGNs (Borghesani et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Borghesani et al., 2002 and Zhou et al., 2007.

claim: In the absence of Shh, BDNF stimulated the migration of CGN.
source: In the absence of Shh, BDNF stimulated the migration of CGN in agreement with the previously mentioned reports (Figure 5C–D)
evidence: Supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: In the presence of Shh, which promotes proliferation and maintains elevated levels of p75NTR, BDNF did not induce migration.
source: whereas, in the presence of Shh, which promotes proliferation and maintains elevated levels of p75NTR, BDNF did not induce migration (Figure 5C–D)
evidence: Supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Only the postmitotic CGNs that have downregulated p75NTR responded to BDNF with increased migration.
source: indicating that only the postmitotic CGNs that have downregulated p75NTR responded to BDNF with increased migration
evidence: Inferred from the data showing BDNF-induced migration only in the absence of Shh (Figure 5C-D).

claim: CGN transfected with a control GFP construct showed an increase in migration in response to BDNF.
source: Our results showed an increase in migration in response to BDNF in the CGN transfected with a control GFP construct (Figure 5E top panel, Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: The chemotactic effect of BDNF was lost in the CGN overexpressing p75NTR.
source: However, the chemotactic effect of BDNF was lost in the CGN overexpressing p75NTR (Figure 5E bottom panel, Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: p75NTR is sufficient to prevent CGN migration even in the presence of a chemotactic signal such as BDNF.
source: suggesting that p75NTR is sufficient to prevent CGN migration even in the presence of a chemotactic signal such as BDNF.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing p75NTR overexpression blocks BDNF-induced migration (Figure 5E-F).

claim: In slices transfected with the Ctrl-GFP vector, cells migrated toward the IGL.
source: In slices transfected with the Ctrl-GFP vector, we observed cells migrating toward the IGL (Figure 5G top panels, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The migration parameters (speed and distance) of Ctrl-GFP transfected cells were consistent with previously reported values.
source: The migration parameters, speed and distance, were consistent with previously reported values (Figure 5H–I; Yacubova and Komuro, 2002).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5H-I and citation to Yacubova and Komuro, 2002.

claim: Ctrl-GFP transfected cells displayed the classic morphology of migrating neurons, with a leading process extended toward the IGL and 'saltatory' migration pattern.
source: These cells displayed the classic morphology of migrating neurons, a leading process extended toward the IGL was observed and the soma showed a 'saltatory' migration pattern, that is, alternating stationary and displacement periods of the cell body (Yacubova and Komuro, 2002).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy observations and citation to Yacubova and Komuro, 2002.

claim: When p75NTR was overexpressed, the transfected neurons remained in the EGL.
source: However, when p75NTR was overexpressed, the transfected neurons remained in the EGL.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: p75NTR-overexpressing cells maintained a rounded morphology and never extended a process in any direction.
source: In contrast to the control conditions, these cells maintained a rounded morphology and never extended a process in any direction, resembling a non-migrating neuron (Figure 5G bottom panels, Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The presence of p75NTR is sufficient to prevent granule cell migration.
source: These results strongly support the possibility that the presence of p75NTR is sufficient to prevent granule cell migration
evidence: Inferred from the data showing p75NTR overexpression blocks migration in organotypic slices (Figure 5G).

claim: The receptor needs to be downregulated before the cells start to migrate.
source: and the receptor needs to be downregulated before the cells start to migrate.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing p75NTR expression prevents migration and is absent in migrating cells (Figures 1, 5).

claim: p75FL/FL; Atoh1Cre mice lack p75NTR expression specifically in the EGL while maintaining WT expression of the receptor in the Purkinje cells.
source: In the cerebellum, these mice lack p75NTR expression specifically in the EGL while maintaining WT expression of the receptor in the Purkinje cells (Zanin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zanin et al., 2016.

claim: At both 24 and 48 hr after EdU injection, a significantly increased number of EdU+ cells were found in the IGL of the p75FL/FL; Atoh1Cre mice compared to WT animals.
source: At both time points, 24 and 48 hr, a significantly increased number of EdU+ cells were found in the IGL of the p75FL/FL; Atoh1Cre mice compared to WT animals (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Supported by EdU labeling and quantification data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: A significant increase of EdU+ cells was observed in the anterior lobes (lobule 5) and the posterior lobes (lobules 6 and 9) of p75FL/FL; Atoh1Cre mice.
source: Developmental differences between anterior and posterior lobes have been previously reported (Martinez et al., 2013), however, we observed a significant increase of EdU+ cells in the anterior lobes (lobule 5) and the posterior lobes (lobules 6 and 9) of p75FL/FL; Atoh1Cre (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: Supported by EdU labeling and quantification data shown in Figure 6C-D and citation to Martinez et al., 2013.

claim: PAX6 staining confirmed the cerebellar granule neuron identity of the EdU+ cells in the IGL.
source: PAX6 staining confirmed the cerebellar granule neuron identity of the EdU+ cells in the IGL (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In WT as well as in p75FL/FL; Atoh1Cre animals, the number of EdU/Ki67 positive cells present in the IGL was close to zero, and no difference was observed between the genotypes.
source: Our results showed that in WT as well as in p75FL/FL; Atoh1Cre animals, the number of EdU/Ki67 positive cells present in the IGL was close to zero, and no difference was observed between the genotypes (Figure 6F–G)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and quantification data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Cell migration of proliferating GCPs was not observed when p75NTR was removed.
source: indicating that cell migration of proliferating GCPs was not observed when we removed p75NTR
evidence: Inferred from the data showing no EdU/Ki67 double-positive cells in the IGL (Figure 6F-G).

claim: Cells still exited the cell cycle before migration when p75NTR was removed.
source: therefore cells still exited the cell cycle before migration.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing no EdU/Ki67 double-positive cells in the IGL (Figure 6F-G).

claim: RhoA activity is known to be regulated by p75NTR.
source: RhoA activity is known to be regulated by p75NTR (Yamashita et al., 1999; Yamashita and Tohyama, 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Yamashita et al., 1999 and Yamashita and Tohyama, 2003.

claim: Granule cells from p75NTRKO mice show reduced levels of active RhoA.
source: and granule cells from p75NTRKO mice show reduced levels of active RhoA (Figure 7A)
evidence: Supported by G-Lisa analysis data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Inhibition of the RhoA pathway significantly increased the number of migrating cells compared to the control condition, even in the absence of a chemoattractant.
source: Even in the absence of a chemoattractant, inhibition of the RhoA pathway significantly increased the number of migrating cells compared to the control condition (Figure 7B, black bars)
evidence: Supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The inhibition of Rho kinase did not affect the ability of BDNF to promote migration.
source: Moreover, the inhibition of Rho kinase did not affect the ability of BDNF to promote migration, suggesting that RhoA is not required for CGN migration (Figure 7B, gray bars).
evidence: Supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: RhoA is not required for CGN migration.
source: suggesting that RhoA is not required for CGN migration (Figure 7B, gray bars)
evidence: Inferred from the data showing RhoA inhibition does not block BDNF-induced migration (Figure 7B).

claim: Organotypic cultures transfected with Ctrl-GFP migrated normally when exposed to a Rho kinase inhibitor.
source: Organotypic cultures transfected with Ctrl-GFP migrated normally when exposed to a Rho kinase inhibitor (Figure 7C and Figure 7—video 1)
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: RhoA activity is not necessary for migration to occur.
source: confirming that RhoA activity is not necessary for migration to occur (compare Figure 5—video 1 and Figure 7—video 1)
evidence: Inferred from the data showing normal migration in the presence of RhoA inhibitor (Figure 7C).

claim: Overexpression of a constitutively active form of RhoA (CA-RhoA) in the EGL of P7 cerebellar slices inhibited migration toward the IGL.
source: However, overexpression of a constitutively active form of RhoA (CA-RhoA) in the EGL of P7 cerebellar slices inhibited migration toward the IGL (Figure 7D and Figure 7—video 2)
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The majority of the cells overexpressing CA-RhoA maintained a rounded shape with no extended process.
source: and the majority of the cells maintained a rounded shape with no extended process in the transfected cells (Figure 7D and Figure 7—video 2)
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The cells expressing the CA-RhoA remained in the EGL, and no GFP was detected in the IGL.
source: The cells expressing the CA-RhoA remained in the EGL, and no GFP was detected in the IGL.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: No colocalization between the CA-RhoA cells and DCX was observed.
source: Consistent with the anti-migratory role of RhoA, no colocalization between the CA-RhoA cells and DCX was observed (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: p75NTR can interact with Rho-GDI at the plasma membrane of GCPs, helping to maintain high levels of active RhoA in a ligand-independent fashion.
source: p75NTR can interact with Rho-GDI at the plasma membrane of GCPs, helping to maintain high levels of active RhoA in a ligand-independent fashion (Yamashita et al., 1999; Yamashita and Tohyama, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yamashita et al., 1999 and Yamashita and Tohyama, 2003.

claim: Active RhoA was necessary for the GCPs to remain in the cell cycle.
source: We have previously demonstrated that active RhoA was necessary for the GCPs to remain in the cell cycle
evidence: Supported by reference to previous work (Zanin et al., 2019).

claim: Inhibition of RhoA elicited cell cycle exit of GCPs, which was correlated with a downregulation of p75NTR.
source: and inhibition of RhoA elicited cell cycle exit of GCPs, which was correlated with a downregulation of p75NTR (Zanin et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zanin et al., 2019.

claim: Inhibiting RhoA was sufficient to induce migration of the CGN overexpressing p75NTR.
source: Our results showed that inhibiting RhoA was sufficient to induce migration of the CGN (Figure 7F and Figure 7—video 3).

claim: The inhibition of CGN migration induced by p75NTR requires the activation of RhoA.
source: These results confirm that the inhibition of CGN migration induced by p75NTR requires the activation of RhoA.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing RhoA inhibition rescues migration in p75NTR-overexpressing cells (Figure 7F).
